summary:
Greenland stands under Denmark's national criminal law and document rules as they apply here. It is a self-governing territory within the Realm of Denmark, with its own parliament and courts for domestic law, while criminal and civil-status legislation originates with the Danish state.

Same-sex partnership has been recognised since 1996, when legislation modelled on the Danish partnership law was adopted with virtually no debate in the local parliament. Marriage equality followed in 2016: the territory adopted Danish legislation that had been passed unanimously twice, the first bill having lapsed because of Danish general elections, and the new law replaced the 1996 partnership regime. The bishop of the established church supported the change.

Also in 2016 Greenland moved to a self-declaration approach to legal gender recognition, ahead of the practice then in force in Denmark itself. A trans visitor therefore arrives in a jurisdiction where identity documents can be corrected without a medical or judicial gatekeeping process under the local rules.

The social picture reported by visitors and press is low-friction. Gay life is described as 'almost a non-event': low-key, integrated and non-violent, with a modest Pride march held since 2010. A national association, LGBT Qaamaneq, was founded in 2014 to work for the political, cultural and social equality of lesbians, gays, bisexuals and transgender people, and it is open to family, friends and colleagues as supporters.

The practical counterweight is capacity rather than hostility. Some 56,000 people are spread across remote settlements and a handful of towns, so specialist services, trans-competent healthcare and a visible community are thin on the ground even where the law is permissive.
tangentialFactors:
Greenland's document rules and gender-recognition practice have at times run ahead of Denmark's, which is unusual for a territory that otherwise inherits the metropole's statutory framework. The self-declaration system adopted in 2016 preceded equivalent reform in Denmark.

Legislative timing in Greenland can be held hostage to Danish politics: the marriage bill lapsed once because of a Danish general election and had to be passed a second time before it could take effect in April 2016.

The established church's public support for same-sex marriage removed the usual institutional opposition seen elsewhere in the Nordic countries, and the 1996 partnership law passed without the polemics that accompanied similar reforms in neighbouring states.

Scale shapes expectations more than legal text does. With a population smaller than most towns, anonymity is limited: a trans visitor in Nuuk or the smaller settlements may be one of very few visible trans people, which cuts both ways in a community described as integrated and non-violent.
localsOnly:
Residents correct their legal gender marker by self-declaration under rules adopted in 2016, without the psychiatric assessment or court petition required in many jurisdictions.

Same-sex couples have had access to marriage since April 2016, replacing the partnership status available from 1996; the change was carried unanimously in the local parliament and supported by the bishop of the established church.

LGBT Qaamaneq, founded in August 2014, is the national association for lesbians, gays, bisexuals and transgender people, pursuing political, cultural and social equality and admitting family, friends and colleagues as supporters. It is a resident organisation rather than a visitor service.

Domestic criminal law and civil-status law are made in Greenland's own parliament for local application, while the overarching criminal and document statutes of the Danish state set the framework within which that legislation operates.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory addresses hate-crime or hate-speech provisions covering gender identity in Greenland, or how such provisions have been enforced; that question is unresolved here.

There is no sourced reporting on violence or harassment directed specifically at trans people in Greenland, nor on police handling of such incidents. The 'non-violent' characterisation comes from a 2015 travel-culture account and is not a crime statistic.

Access to gender-affirming medical care, referral routes and waiting times are not covered by the inventory; the self-declaration rule concerns legal documents only.

Entry and visa requirements for Greenland are not stated in the sources reviewed, and neither are the specific document-marker formats used on local identity papers.

The population figure and settlement description derive from general background rather than a dated official census in this inventory.
